script.opening: "Alright doc. My knee's come up massive and it's really sore — I reckon I twisted it at football last week. Could you give me some strong anti-inflammatories or maybe drain it? It's killing me. There's no need for a big examination or anything, I just need it sorted so I can get back to five-a-side. It's just a footy knee, right?"

facts.text: Right knee, swollen over four days, warm, sore — 6/10. You can walk on it with a limp and bend it about halfway. If asked about football: you played last Thursday but cannot remember a twist or a tackle. On video: the right knee is visibly bigger than the left.
The back of your left heel has been sore for a week, especially first thing.
No fever, no shakes; feel well in yourself. Checked your temperature this morning: 37.4°C. No rash. No other joints hot or swollen.

facts.topic: Gut — only if asked about recent illness or travel
facts.text: Three weeks ago in Ibiza you had "bad food poisoning" — diarrhoea with some blood for three days. It settled on its own.
Both eyes were red and gritty last week, settled now. A bit of stinging when you pass urine for about a week. No discharge you have noticed.

facts.topic: Sex — only if asked sensitively and with a reason
facts.text: "There was a girl on the holiday. We didn't use anything." You have a girlfriend at home; you have had sex with her since you got back. You are embarrassed and anxious about this.
Nothing. No medicines. No allergies. No injections into the joint. No IV drug use.
27, electrician. Lives alone, girlfriend Chloe stays over often. Smoke socially, drink at weekends.

Cheerful, keen to minimise. Steer back to football. If the doctor asks about your love life in a judgemental way, deny anything. If they explain why they are asking (this kind of swollen knee can follow an infection, including from sex) and keep it confidential, tell them. Then ask anxiously: "Do I have to tell Chloe?" Accept being seen in person today if the doctor explains they need to check it is not an infected joint.

ice.ideas: "It's a footy knee — I must have twisted it."
ice.concerns: Underneath (only if asked): that you have caught something on holiday and passed it to Chloe.
ice.expectations: "Strong anti-inflammatories or drain it." You will accept tests and an in-person check if they are explained and kept confidential.

cues: "It's just a footy knee, right?" — say in the opening.
"I did have a bad stomach bug on holiday." — say if asked about recent illness.
"Is this going to go any further?" — ask before talking about sex.

checkpoints.text: Excludes SEPTIC ARTHRITIS first: recognises a hot, swollen, acutely painful single joint as a potential joint-destroying emergency — assesses for fever/systemic upset/inability to weight-bear and a very hot joint, and arranges urgent assessment ± joint aspiration if a septic picture — rather than just giving NSAIDs/draining for a "twisted knee"

Recognises the REACTIVE ARTHRITIS pattern: acute (oligo)arthritis (often a knee) days–weeks after a GI (dysentery) or STI trigger, ± enthesitis (Achilles/heel), conjunctivitis and urethritis ("can’t see, can’t pee, can’t climb a tree")

Takes a thorough, NON-JUDGEMENTAL history that elicits BOTH the recent GI infection AND the sexual history (new partner, unprotected sex) — recognising the patient will not volunteer the sexual trigger — plus the eye and urinary symptoms

Arranges an STI SCREEN (chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT, full screen) and PARTNER NOTIFICATION if an STI trigger is found/likely, treats chlamydia if confirmed, and assesses/manages conjunctivitis and urethritis

Manages the reactive arthritis appropriately once sepsis excluded: NSAIDs ± intra-articular corticosteroid, explains it is usually self-limiting (weeks–months), HLA-B27 association, and refers/escalates if severe, persistent or diagnostic uncertainty

Creates a safe, non-judgemental space (and the right to be seen alone / asked sensitively) so the hidden sexual history can be disclosed, rather than accepting the "football" explanation and resistance to examination
Handles the embarrassment/guilt and partner-notification conversation with compassion and without moralising, so the STI trigger is addressed

Safety-nets and follows up: urgent assessment/aspiration if any septic features, the STI screen/partner notification and arthritis management, eye/urinary review, return advice if worsening/fever, and a follow-up — excluding the emergency and treating the real cause

worked.txt: "Before we call it a footy knee, I have to be careful: a hot, swollen, very painful joint that came up without a real injury, I always have to make sure there’s no infection IN the joint, because that’s an emergency that can damage it fast. So I do need to examine it properly, and if it looks infected we get it assessed and possibly a sample taken today — that comes first."

"Now, you mentioned your heel’s sore too. Can I ask — have you had any tummy upset recently, like a bad case of the runs? … On holiday, three weeks ago. That’s really relevant. There’s a type of joint inflammation that flares up a few weeks AFTER an infection — it’s called reactive arthritis, and a knee like this with a sore Achilles fits it well."

"I need to ask some personal questions, and there’s zero judgement — it’s just that this can also be triggered by an infection caught through sex. On that holiday, was there any new sexual partner, any unprotected sex? … Thank you for being honest, genuinely. That’s really useful, because it points to the likely trigger and something we can test for and treat."

"Two quick things that go with this — any gritty or red eyes, and any stinging or discharge passing water? … A bit, yeah. Those fit the same picture. None of this is anything to be ashamed of — it’s a known reaction, and it’s manageable."

"So the plan: I’ll make sure the knee isn’t infected, and do a sexual-health screen — all confidential — and if we find an infection like chlamydia we treat it, and your recent partner would need testing too, which the clinic can help with. For the knee itself, anti-inflammatories and sometimes a steroid injection settle it; it usually clears over a few weeks."

"If the knee gets much hotter, you spike a fever, or you can’t weight-bear at all — that’s straight back to us or A&E, because that would worry me about infection. Otherwise I’ll sort the tests and treatment and see you to follow up. You came in for a footy knee; what it actually is, is something we can name, treat, and sort properly — including the bits you almost didn’t mention."

f.learning: A hot, swollen, acutely painful single joint with no real injury must ALWAYS have SEPTIC ARTHRITIS excluded first — a joint-destroying emergency — so urgent assessment ± joint aspiration is the safe pathway for a genuinely hot/septic-looking joint, not NSAIDs/drainage for a "twisted knee". The likely diagnosis here is REACTIVE ARTHRITIS: an acute (oligo)arthritis (often a knee) days–weeks after a GI (dysentery) or STI trigger, ± enthesitis (Achilles/heel), conjunctivitis and urethritis ("can’t see, can’t pee, can’t climb a tree"), HLA-B27-associated and usually self-limiting. The examinable hidden agenda is the unvoiced sexual trigger — unprotected sex with a new partner the patient won’t disclose — which is directly relevant (chlamydia) and needs a non-judgemental sexual history, an STI screen and partner notification. Take a thorough history eliciting BOTH the GI infection and the sexual history (and the eye/urinary symptoms), exclude sepsis, screen/treat the STI and notify partners, manage the arthritis (NSAIDs ± intra-articular steroid), and safety-net septic features.

knowledge.guideline: BSR/BHPR hot swollen joint guideline (2006) · BASHH Chlamydia trachomatis guideline (2026) · BASHH gonorrhoea guideline (2025) · NICE NG253
knowledge.summary: An acutely hot, swollen knee without real injury is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Once that is excluded, a knee plus heel pain weeks after dysentery or unprotected sex is reactive arthritis, and the trigger must be found and treated.

points.t: BSR/BHPR 2006: an acute hot swollen joint is septic until proven otherwise. Aspirate before antibiotics where possible and send for Gram stain, culture and crystals. Fever and systemic upset may be absent. A hot, swollen joint that cannot be examined in person needs a same-day face-to-face assessment.

A sterile, usually asymmetrical oligoarthritis of large lower-limb joints, starting days to weeks after a gastrointestinal (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia) or genitourinary (Chlamydia trachomatis) infection. It may come with enthesitis (Achilles, heel), conjunctivitis or anterior uveitis, and urethritis. It is associated with HLA-B27.

Ask about recent diarrhoea and take a sexual history: new partners, condom use, symptoms of urethritis, and the partner’s status. Men often won’t volunteer it. Offer to see him alone and explain why you are asking.

Offer chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT (first-void urine), plus HIV and syphilis tests, ideally through sexual health services. BASHH 2026: first-line treatment for uncomplicated chlamydia is doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. Gonorrhoea is managed through sexual health (BASHH 2025).

A sexual health adviser decides the look-back period and can notify contacts anonymously. BASHH 2026 uses 4 weeks before symptom onset for men with urethral symptoms. Advise no sex until he and his partners have completed treatment.

Once sepsis is excluded: NSAIDs (dose per BNF), with intra-articular steroid for a persistent single joint. Most cases settle over weeks to months. Refer to rheumatology if severe, persistent or uncertain. A red, painful eye with photophobia or blurred vision needs same-day ophthalmology to exclude uveitis.

dg.d: Open question; let him make the ‘footy knee’ case, then tested the injury story rather than accepting it.
Explored the holiday, the new partner, the girlfriend at home, and what he fears about disclosure.
Same-day face-to-face exam; aspiration via hospital if septic features; chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, HIV and syphilis serology.
Septic arthritis versus reactive arthritis (post-dysenteric or post-chlamydial) versus disseminated gonococcal infection, gout or injury.
Asked about fever, systemic upset and weight-bearing; arranged in-person assessment because a hot joint can’t be excluded on video; checked eyes for uveitis.
Named probable reactive arthritis, with the GI and sexual triggers and the triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis and urethritis.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

model.text: Hi Jordan, thanks for joining. Tell me what’s been happening with your knee.

It’s come up massive and it’s killing me. I reckon I twisted it at football. Can you just give me strong anti-inflammatories, or drain it? I don’t need a big examination. It’s just a footy knee, right?

I can see it’s really painful, and I want to get you sorted. I’ll ask a few focused questions to make sure it is just a footy knee, because some swollen knees need something different. Then we’ll agree a plan. Fair?
model.why: Acknowledges his request and sets the agenda

model.text: Go on then.
What exactly happened at football — did you feel it twist or pop, and could you carry on?
Honestly… I don’t remember a specific moment. It just swelled up a few days after.
That’s useful. Can you point the camera at both knees? … The right one does look swollen. Is it hot to touch? Can you put weight on it? Any fever, shivers or feeling unwell?
It’s warm, yeah. I can hobble on it. I don’t feel ill — it’s just the knee.
Any pain anywhere else — other joints, your back, your heels?
model.why: Looks for enthesitis and other joints

model.text: Now you say it, my heel’s sore, at the back. I thought that was from limping.

A swollen knee plus a sore heel, without a clear injury, makes me think about something called reactive arthritis. It can follow an infection a few weeks earlier. Have you had any tummy upset recently?
model.why: Forms a hypothesis and searches for the trigger

model.text: Yeah, about three weeks ago. Bad food poisoning on a lads’ holiday. Diarrhoea for days, blood in it once. It’s gone now.

That fits well. The other common trigger is an infection caught through sex. I ask everyone this in this situation, and there’s no judgement at all. Is it OK if I ask a few personal questions? Are you somewhere private?
model.why: Signposts sensitive questions and checks privacy

model.text: (pause) I’m on my own, yeah.
Since that holiday, or on it, have you had sex with anyone new, and was a condom used?
(long pause) …Yeah. Someone on the trip. No condom. I’ve got a girlfriend at home. That’s why I didn’t say.

Thank you for telling me. That can’t have been easy, and everything you tell me stays confidential. It’s really useful, because it helps me treat the right thing. Any stinging when you pass urine, or any discharge? Any gritty or red eyes?
model.why: Thanks him, reassures on confidentiality, completes the triad

model.text: A bit of stinging, yeah. And my eyes were gritty last week. I thought it was hay fever.
And what’s been going through your mind about all of this?
Honestly, I’ve been trying not to think about it. I just wanted the knee sorted. If it’s something from that trip… my girlfriend…
I can hear that’s weighing on you. Let’s take it one step at a time. My job is to look after your health, not to judge.

Here’s what I think. The most likely explanation is reactive arthritis: the immune system reacting to an infection a few weeks ago — either the food poisoning, or an infection like chlamydia caught through sex. The joint itself isn’t infected, and it usually settles.
model.why: Explains the working diagnosis in plain terms

model.text: So it’s not from football?

It doesn’t look like it. But there’s one thing I must rule out first. Rarely, a hot, swollen knee means germs inside the joint, which can damage it quickly. I can’t judge that fully on video, so I’d like to see you in person today. If it looks infected, you’d go to hospital to have fluid drawn off and tested.
model.why: Same-day face-to-face assessment to exclude septic arthritis

model.text: Today? OK. I can get there.

Good. I’ll also arrange a sexual health check: a urine test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, and blood tests for HIV and syphilis. The local sexual health clinic can do all of this confidentially, and they’re very good at this.
model.why: Full STI screen with appropriate referral

model.text: And if it’s chlamydia?

It’s treated with a week of antibiotics. Until you and any partners have finished treatment, no sex, including with your girlfriend. Anyone you’ve slept with recently will need testing too. The clinic has health advisers who can tell partners anonymously, if you prefer.
Anonymous? That… helps. I need to think about what to tell her.
That’s your decision, and it’s understandable to need time. I won’t share anything without your agreement. The clinic can help you think it through too.

For the knee: once infection is ruled out, anti-inflammatory tablets help, and sometimes a steroid injection. Most people recover over weeks to a few months. It’s not a footy knee, so I’d rest from five-a-side until it has settled.
Fair enough.

A few things to act on straight away: if the knee gets much hotter or more swollen, you get a fever or shivers, or you can’t put weight on it, go to A&E. If an eye becomes painful and red, light hurts, or your vision blurs, get seen that day.
model.why: Specific safety-net for sepsis and uveitis

model.text: Got it.
Can you tell me back what the plan is, so I know I’ve explained it properly?
See you today for the knee. Sexual health tests. No sex till it’s sorted. Anti-inflammatories if it’s not infected. A&E if it gets worse or I get a fever.
Perfect. I’ll see you this afternoon, and we’ll follow up once the results are back. Thank you for being honest — it made a real difference.

social.t: Unprotected sex with a new partner while in a relationship brings shame and fear of discovery. This is why he blames football. A non-judgemental approach makes disclosure possible.
He wants to get back to five-a-side. Explain that rest is needed while the joint is inflamed. A fit note may be needed if his job involves heavy physical work.

legal.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017): his sexual history and STI results are confidential. The GP must not tell his girlfriend. Anonymous partner notification through sexual health services protects both confidentiality and public health.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): do not let personal views about a patient’s lifestyle affect care. Explain why sexual history is clinically relevant.
A hot swollen joint can’t be safely assessed on video. Recognise this and arrange in-person review the same day. Document the reasoning.

community.t: Local sexual health (GUM) clinics offer free, confidential testing, treatment and health-adviser partner notification. Many areas also offer online self-sampling kits.

redFlags: Fever, rigors, systemic upset, inability to weight-bear or a very hot joint — septic arthritis; same-day hospital assessment
Painful red eye, photophobia or blurred vision — anterior uveitis; same-day ophthalmology
Rash, pustules or migratory joint pains after new sexual contact — disseminated gonococcal infection
psychosocial: New sexual partner on holiday while in a relationship — guilt and fear of disclosure
Wants to get back to football quickly
Whether he feels able to attend sexual health services
ice: Idea: “I twisted it at football — it’s a footy knee.”
Concern: that the knee is linked to sex on holiday, and what it means for his girlfriend
Expectation: strong anti-inflammatories or drainage, with no examination

playbook.diagnosis: Explain both parts: “This is most likely reactive arthritis — the immune system reacting to an infection a few weeks ago, from the food poisoning or from an infection caught through sex. But first I must rule out an infection inside the joint, so I need to see you in person today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your immune system fought off a bug a few weeks ago, but it’s still on alert and has started inflaming your knee and heel by mistake. It’s like a smoke alarm that keeps going after the fire’s out. It usually settles, but we need to treat any bug that’s still there.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted the knee sorted without the personal questions, and I understand why. Being honest about the trip means we can treat the actual cause.”
management.psychosocial: Keep the tone non-judgemental. Offer anonymous partner notification. Leave the decision about what to tell his girlfriend with him, and advise abstinence until treatment is complete.
sharedPlan: Same-day face-to-face assessment; hospital aspiration if septic features (BSR/BHPR 2006)
Chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, HIV and syphilis via sexual health; treat per BASHH 2026 and 2025
NSAIDs once sepsis excluded; rest from football; rheumatology if persistent or severe
safetyNet: A&E if the knee gets hotter or more swollen, fever or shivers, or he cannot weight-bear
Same-day eye review for a painful red eye, photophobia or blurred vision; follow-up with results

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by accepting the patient’s explanation, missing the septic joint, or never getting to the sexual history. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: Accepting ‘twisted it at football’ and prescribing NSAIDs over video.
items.why: An acutely hot swollen joint is septic until proven otherwise (BSR/BHPR 2006). Video cannot exclude it.
items.fix: “I need to see this knee in person today, to make sure there’s no infection inside the joint.”

items.fail: Not asking about recent diarrhoea or other joints.
items.why: The heel pain and the dysentery three weeks earlier are what point to reactive arthritis.
items.fix: Ask: “Any pain elsewhere, like your heels? Any tummy upset in the last month?”

items.fail: Skipping the sexual history because he seems embarrassed, or asking it in a judgemental way.
items.why: Chlamydia is a common trigger and he won’t volunteer it. Poor wording shuts down disclosure.
items.fix: Signpost, normalise and check privacy: “I ask everyone this. Is it OK to ask some personal questions?”

items.fail: Testing only for chlamydia, or forgetting partner notification.
items.why: A full STI screen includes gonorrhoea, HIV and syphilis. Untreated partners mean reinfection and onward spread.
items.fix: Refer to sexual health for a full screen, treatment and health-adviser partner notification, including anonymous options.

items.fail: Telling him he must tell his girlfriend.
items.why: It breaches his autonomy and may stop him engaging with testing at all.
items.fix: “What you tell her is your decision. The clinic can help, and can notify people anonymously.”

items.fail: Ignoring the gritty eyes and stinging urine.
items.why: These complete the picture, and a red painful eye may be uveitis, which needs same-day ophthalmology.
items.fix: Ask directly, and safety-net: “A painful red eye, light hurting or blurred vision — get seen that day.”

items.fail: A vague ‘come back if it gets worse’ close.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement, and septic arthritis can progress within hours.
items.fix: Name it: “Hotter, more swollen, fever, or you can’t stand on it — go to A&E.”

timeMap.d: He wants NSAIDs or drainage and no examination. Acknowledge it; don’t accept ‘footy knee’ yet.
Mechanism, heat, weight-bearing, fever. Other joints and the heel. Recent diarrhoea.
Signpost, check privacy, ask directly and without judgement. Then urethral and eye symptoms.
Reactive arthritis likely, but see him in person today to exclude septic arthritis. STI screen, partner notification, abstinence. NSAIDs once sepsis excluded.
A&E for hotter joint, fever or not weight-bearing. Same-day eye review for a painful red eye. Teach-back.

wordPics.pass: Considers septic arthritis and arranges assessment; links the knee to the recent diarrhoea; takes a sexual history and offers an STI screen; gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: signposts and normalises the sexual history so he discloses; completes the triad (eyes, urethra); arranges same-day in-person assessment; explains partner notification and anonymous options; respects his control over what he tells his girlfriend; names uveitis symptoms; teach-back confirms the plan.

SCA_MODELS.text: Today? OK. I can get there.

Good. I’ll also arrange a sexual health check: a urine test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, and blood tests for HIV and syphilis. The local sexual health clinic can do all of this confidentially, and they’re very good at this.
SCA_MODELS.why: Full STI screen with appropriate referral

SCA_MODELS.text: And if it’s chlamydia?

It’s treated with a week of antibiotics. Until you and any partners have finished treatment, no sex, including with your girlfriend. Anyone you’ve slept with recently will need testing too. The clinic has health advisers who can tell partners anonymously, if you prefer.
Anonymous? That… helps. I need to think about what to tell her.
That’s your decision, and it’s understandable to need time. I won’t share anything without your agreement. The clinic can help you think it through too.

For the knee: once infection is ruled out, anti-inflammatory tablets help, and sometimes a steroid injection. Most people recover over weeks to a few months. It’s not a footy knee, so I’d rest from five-a-side until it has settled.
Fair enough.

A few things to act on straight away: if the knee gets much hotter or more swollen, you get a fever or shivers, or you can’t put weight on it, go to A&E. If an eye becomes painful and red, light hurts, or your vision blurs, get seen that day.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net for sepsis and uveitis

SCA_MODELS.text: Got it.
Can you tell me back what the plan is, so I know I’ve explained it properly?
See you today for the knee. Sexual health tests. No sex till it’s sorted. Anti-inflammatories if it’s not infected. A&E if it gets worse or I get a fever.
Perfect. I’ll see you this afternoon, and we’ll follow up once the results are back. Thank you for being honest — it made a real difference.

SCA_STEM.name: Jordan Eze
SCA_STEM.recent: Few days of a painful, swollen right knee with no clear injury. No previous joint problems recorded.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation: “my knee’s come up massive — I think I twisted it at football.” Wants anti-inflammatories or for it to be drained.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: BSR/BHPR hot swollen joint guideline (2006) · BASHH Chlamydia trachomatis guideline (2026) · BASHH gonorrhoea guideline (2025) · NICE NG253
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: An acutely hot, swollen knee without real injury is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Once that is excluded, a knee plus heel pain weeks after dysentery or unprotected sex is reactive arthritis, and the trigger must be found and treated.

points.t: BSR/BHPR 2006: an acute hot swollen joint is septic until proven otherwise. Aspirate before antibiotics where possible and send for Gram stain, culture and crystals. Fever and systemic upset may be absent. A hot, swollen joint that cannot be examined in person needs a same-day face-to-face assessment.

A sterile, usually asymmetrical oligoarthritis of large lower-limb joints, starting days to weeks after a gastrointestinal (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia) or genitourinary (Chlamydia trachomatis) infection. It may come with enthesitis (Achilles, heel), conjunctivitis or anterior uveitis, and urethritis. It is associated with HLA-B27.

Ask about recent diarrhoea and take a sexual history: new partners, condom use, symptoms of urethritis, and the partner’s status. Men often won’t volunteer it. Offer to see him alone and explain why you are asking.

Offer chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT (first-void urine), plus HIV and syphilis tests, ideally through sexual health services. BASHH 2026: first-line treatment for uncomplicated chlamydia is doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. Gonorrhoea is managed through sexual health (BASHH 2025).

A sexual health adviser decides the look-back period and can notify contacts anonymously. BASHH 2026 uses 4 weeks before symptom onset for men with urethral symptoms. Advise no sex until he and his partners have completed treatment.

Once sepsis is excluded: NSAIDs (dose per BNF), with intra-articular steroid for a persistent single joint. Most cases settle over weeks to months. Refer to rheumatology if severe, persistent or uncertain. A red, painful eye with photophobia or blurred vision needs same-day ophthalmology to exclude uveitis.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him make the ‘footy knee’ case, then tested the injury story rather than accepting it.
Explored the holiday, the new partner, the girlfriend at home, and what he fears about disclosure.
Picked up ‘I don’t remember a specific moment’, the heel pain and the hesitation, and followed each.
Idea (twisted at football); concern (the new partner and his girlfriend); expectation (NSAIDs or drainage).
Same-day face-to-face exam; aspiration via hospital if septic features; chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, HIV and syphilis serology.
Septic arthritis versus reactive arthritis (post-dysenteric or post-chlamydial) versus disseminated gonococcal infection, gout or injury.
Asked about fever, systemic upset and weight-bearing; arranged in-person assessment because a hot joint can’t be excluded on video; checked eyes for uveitis.
Named probable reactive arthritis, with the GI and sexual triggers and the triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis and urethritis.
Sepsis excluded first; STI screen via sexual health; chlamydia treated per BASHH 2026; NSAIDs once sepsis excluded; rest from football.
Partner notification through a health adviser; abstinence until treatment complete; eye and urinary symptoms addressed.
A&E for hotter joint, fever or inability to weight-bear; same-day eye review for pain, photophobia or blurred vision; follow-up with results.

social.t: Unprotected sex with a new partner while in a relationship brings shame and fear of discovery. This is why he blames football. A non-judgemental approach makes disclosure possible.
He wants to get back to five-a-side. Explain that rest is needed while the joint is inflamed. A fit note may be needed if his job involves heavy physical work.

legal.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017): his sexual history and STI results are confidential. The GP must not tell his girlfriend. Anonymous partner notification through sexual health services protects both confidentiality and public health.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): do not let personal views about a patient’s lifestyle affect care. Explain why sexual history is clinically relevant.
A hot swollen joint can’t be safely assessed on video. Recognise this and arrange in-person review the same day. Document the reasoning.

community.t: Local sexual health (GUM) clinics offer free, confidential testing, treatment and health-adviser partner notification. Many areas also offer online self-sampling kits.

redFlags: Fever, rigors, systemic upset, inability to weight-bear or a very hot joint — septic arthritis; same-day hospital assessment
Painful red eye, photophobia or blurred vision — anterior uveitis; same-day ophthalmology
Rash, pustules or migratory joint pains after new sexual contact — disseminated gonococcal infection
psychosocial: New sexual partner on holiday while in a relationship — guilt and fear of disclosure
Wants to get back to football quickly
Whether he feels able to attend sexual health services
ice: Idea: “I twisted it at football — it’s a footy knee.”
Concern: that the knee is linked to sex on holiday, and what it means for his girlfriend
Expectation: strong anti-inflammatories or drainage, with no examination

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Explain both parts: “This is most likely reactive arthritis — the immune system reacting to an infection a few weeks ago, from the food poisoning or from an infection caught through sex. But first I must rule out an infection inside the joint, so I need to see you in person today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your immune system fought off a bug a few weeks ago, but it’s still on alert and has started inflaming your knee and heel by mistake. It’s like a smoke alarm that keeps going after the fire’s out. It usually settles, but we need to treat any bug that’s still there.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted the knee sorted without the personal questions, and I understand why. Being honest about the trip means we can treat the actual cause.”
management.psychosocial: Keep the tone non-judgemental. Offer anonymous partner notification. Leave the decision about what to tell his girlfriend with him, and advise abstinence until treatment is complete.
sharedPlan: Same-day face-to-face assessment; hospital aspiration if septic features (BSR/BHPR 2006)
Chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, HIV and syphilis via sexual health; treat per BASHH 2026 and 2025
NSAIDs once sepsis excluded; rest from football; rheumatology if persistent or severe
safetyNet: A&E if the knee gets hotter or more swollen, fever or shivers, or he cannot weight-bear
Same-day eye review for a painful red eye, photophobia or blurred vision; follow-up with results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by accepting the patient’s explanation, missing the septic joint, or never getting to the sexual history. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: Accepting ‘twisted it at football’ and prescribing NSAIDs over video.
items.why: An acutely hot swollen joint is septic until proven otherwise (BSR/BHPR 2006). Video cannot exclude it.
items.fix: “I need to see this knee in person today, to make sure there’s no infection inside the joint.”

items.fail: Not asking about recent diarrhoea or other joints.
items.why: The heel pain and the dysentery three weeks earlier are what point to reactive arthritis.
items.fix: Ask: “Any pain elsewhere, like your heels? Any tummy upset in the last month?”

items.fail: Skipping the sexual history because he seems embarrassed, or asking it in a judgemental way.
items.why: Chlamydia is a common trigger and he won’t volunteer it. Poor wording shuts down disclosure.
items.fix: Signpost, normalise and check privacy: “I ask everyone this. Is it OK to ask some personal questions?”

items.fail: Testing only for chlamydia, or forgetting partner notification.
items.why: A full STI screen includes gonorrhoea, HIV and syphilis. Untreated partners mean reinfection and onward spread.
items.fix: Refer to sexual health for a full screen, treatment and health-adviser partner notification, including anonymous options.

items.fail: Telling him he must tell his girlfriend.
items.why: It breaches his autonomy and may stop him engaging with testing at all.
items.fix: “What you tell her is your decision. The clinic can help, and can notify people anonymously.”

items.fail: Ignoring the gritty eyes and stinging urine.
items.why: These complete the picture, and a red painful eye may be uveitis, which needs same-day ophthalmology.
items.fix: Ask directly, and safety-net: “A painful red eye, light hurting or blurred vision — get seen that day.”

items.fail: A vague ‘come back if it gets worse’ close.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement, and septic arthritis can progress within hours.
items.fix: Name it: “Hotter, more swollen, fever, or you can’t stand on it — go to A&E.”
